evidence.title: Optimizing AI implementation for surgery: recommendations for infrastructure and deployment in the operating room
evidence.outcome: Estimated operational carbon emissions of cloud versus edge deployment
evidence.effect: Cloud emitted ~26.22 g CO 2 e every hour during inference, versus 6.84 g CO 2 e for Edge; idle Edge emissions were 3.8 g CO 2 e every hour.

evidence.title: Quantifying the Relationship Between Clinical Safety and Environmental Impact in Therapeutic LLMs
evidence.outcome: Environmental cost (energy, carbon, water, abiotic depletion) versus clinical safety score across LLM configurations
evidence.effect: 2.61 percentage-point increase in clinical safety score corresponded to about 60-fold increase in estimated energy use per million output tokens; extra test-time compute did not consistently improve safety.
evidence.quote: The results indicate a non-linear trade-off at the upper end of the safety distribution: a 2.61 percentage-point increase in clinical safety score corresponded to an approximately 60-fold increase in estimated energy use per million output tokens.

commentary.bottom_line: One vignette study of 513 participants in China found that a provider described as using proactive ethics practices received higher patient attitude ratings, but no study tested whether impact assessment reduces ethical, social, environmental, or workforce harms. Three hazard studies show that AI tools carry measurable energy and carbon costs, which supports the concern but does not show that the practice addresses it.

perspectives.view: A single vignette study (n=513) is the only test of the practice, and it reported attitude means of 5.67 versus 4.28. Its outcome is indirect because attitudes stand in for harms, the setting is simulated, and no replication exists. Certainty is very low, and the three environmental studies document the hazard rather than test the practice.

No study measured whether a pre-deployment assessment caught an ethical, social, or workforce harm before it reached patients. One estimate puts worldwide yearly emissions from digital pathology deep learning at up to 16 Mt. Another found a 60-fold energy increase for a 2.61 percentage-point safety gain, which suggests more compute may not yield more safety.

A simulation involving 23 clinicians estimated about 26.22 g CO2e per hour for cloud inference versus 6.84 g for edge deployment. This suggests deployment architecture is one factor an assessment could examine. The study did not test whether an assessment changed architecture choices or how much staff time such a review requires.

Across 47 model configurations, extra test-time compute did not consistently improve safety scores, which suggests smaller configurations may lower energy use with limited safety loss. No study reports the cost, staffing, or time needed to run ethical and workforce impact reviews at scale, so resourcing plans currently rest on endorsements alone.

None of the four studies enrolled or analyzed Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy groups. The attitude study drew participants in China, and the environmental studies used slides, clinicians, or benchmarks. Whether impact assessments detect harms that fall on these populations has not been tested.

Participants rated a provider higher when it described proactive ethics practices in the vignette. This suggests openness about impact review may support trust. The study measured reactions to a written scenario, so it does not show whether patients were protected from harm or could reach a human when a tool raised concerns.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares deployments with and without structured ethical, social, environmental, and workforce impact assessment. Such studies would need to run in operating health systems and measure downstream patient harms, workforce effects such as staff burden or displacement, energy and carbon use, and the cost of conducting the reviews.
commentary.underserved_note: No test of the practice included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The single attitude study used a general sample in China, so health systems serving these groups have no direct evidence that impact assessment identifies or reduces harms concentrated among their patients.
